title: Floating point, tolerances, and why 1e-6 matters

questions.stem: A test model has two rows that no point satisfies together: x + y <= 1 and x + y >= 1.0000003. HiGHS solves it with its default settings twice, once as an LP and once with x declared integer. What should you expect?

options.text: Both runs report INFEASIBLE, since no point satisfies both rows exactly
options.says: Solvers accept rows broken by less than their tolerance; the MIP run's tolerance is 1e-6, above 3e-7.

options.text: The LP run reports INFEASIBLE and the MIP run OPTIMAL, since HiGHS checks MIPs more loosely
options.says: Right: HiGHS's LP tolerance is 1e-7 and its MIP tolerance 1e-6, so only the MIP run accepts a row broken by 3e-7.

options.text: Both runs report OPTIMAL, since every solver accepts rows broken by up to 1e-6
options.says: HiGHS's LP tolerance is 1e-7: it refused rows 5e-7 apart.

options.text: The LP run reports OPTIMAL and the MIP run INFEASIBLE, since HiGHS checks MIPs more strictly
options.says: It is the other way round: the MIP tolerance, 1e-6, is the looser one.

origin.section: A Solver Accepts a Row Broken by Less Than Its Feasibility Tolerance

questions.stem: A council's budget model is checked with HiGHS's default MIP tolerance. A test plan overspends a $4.2M budget by $300, and with the budget row written in $k the check refuses it. The team rewrites the row in $B. What does the check do now?

options.text: It refuses the plan, since a tolerance is the same amount of money in any unit
options.says: A tolerance is a number in the row's units: 1e-6 is a tenth of a cent in $k and $1,000 in $B.

options.text: It refuses the plan, since HiGHS measures the overspend against the row's size
options.says: That is SCIP's relative comparison; HiGHS's verdicts matched an absolute tolerance in every unit.

options.text: It allows the plan, since floats near a few thousandths are spaced wider than $300
options.says: The gap between floats shrinks with the number; near 0.0042 it is far below $300 in any unit.

options.text: It allows the plan, since a millionth of a billion dollars is more than $300
options.says: Right: in $B a tolerance of 1e-6 is $1,000, so a $300 overspend passes.

origin.section: A Tolerance Is Measured in the Row's Units, So Its Worth in Money Depends on Them

questions.stem: A switch row reads loan <= M * arranged, with M = 1e8 in $k. The solver returns arranged = 4e-7 with a loan of $40,000k and reports OPTIMAL. A planner rounds every binary before reading the plan. What is the planner's plan?

options.text: No loan is arranged, so the loan goes and some budget rows can break
options.says: Right: 4e-7 rounds to 0, the loan disappears with it, and any year that relied on it overspends.

options.text: A loan is arranged, so the plan pays its fee and keeps its value
options.says: 4e-7 rounds to 0, not 1: the plan has no loan arranged.

options.text: The solver's plan is unchanged, since rounding by 4e-7 never matters
options.says: 4e-7 times 1e8 is the whole $40,000k loan: rounding removes it.

options.text: The plan breaks every budget row, since rounding always overspends
options.says: Only years that relied on the loan overspend; in the lesson, 2027 borrowed and still fit its budget.

origin.section: A Binary Within the Integrality Tolerance Counts as Whole, and Rounding It Changes the Plan
